title: Philemon
tagline: A short, personal letter from prison: Paul sends a slave back to his master and asks that he be received as a brother.
author: Paul
authorNote: Paul names himself as writer (1:1, 1:9, 1:19) and signs "with my own hand" (1:19). Almost no scholar doubts that Paul wrote it; it is one of the seven letters most widely accepted as his. Timothy is named with him in the greeting.
audience: Philemon, a believer and host of a house church, with Apphia, Archippus, and the assembly that meets in his house
audienceNote: Philemon is probably the head of a household in Colossae: Onesimus is described as "one of you" in Colossians 4:9, and Archippus, named in the greeting, is mentioned in Colossians 4:17. The letter is addressed to Philemon but is read to the whole assembly, since "you" in 1:3 and 1:25 is plural.
setting: Paul in prison, probably in Rome, perhaps about AD 60 to 62
settingNote: Paul calls himself a "prisoner of Christ Jesus" (1:1, 1:9) and expects to be released and to visit (1:22). Rome (Acts 28:30) is the traditional place. Some scholars have proposed Ephesus (where a stay in prison is likely but not recorded) or Caesarea (Acts 24-26), mostly because Colossae is a long way from Rome and Paul's expected visit seems close. The letter is sent along with Colossians (Colossians 4:7-9).
genreNote: The shortest of Paul's letters, and the only one from him on a purely private matter. It follows the usual shape of a letter (greeting, thanks, request, closing greetings) and uses persuasion, not command: Paul says he could order but would rather "beg for love's sake" (1:8-9).
bigIdea: A runaway or separated slave, Onesimus, has become a believer through Paul in prison. Paul sends him back with this letter, asking Philemon to receive him "no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother," and to put any debt on Paul's account. The gospel changes the way two people stand to each other.
themes: Brothers in Christ, whatever else they are
Love as the basis of an appeal
Paul's offer to pay a debt
Slavery in the Roman world, and the questions the letter leaves open
mapSummary: Philemon lived in Colossae; Paul writes from prison, traditionally in Rome.

scene.author: Paul, in prison
scene.audience: Philemon and the church in his house at Colossae
scene.happening: Onesimus is being sent back with a letter, probably about AD 60 to 62
